entry:
Intentional human activity undertaken to meet one's own needs and wants, or those of others or of organizations. In economics, work is human labor that, alongside other factors of production, contributes to the creation of [[Goods|goods]] and services. It exists in all human societies, paid or unpaid, from gathering resources by hand in [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherer]] groups to operating complex technologies in industrial and post-industrial societies. A person's regular role in work is an occupation, or job. Societies coordinate work through institutions such as government programs, nonprofit organizations, cooperatives, and corporations.

What counts as work depends on context. Sport is a job for a professional athlete but a [[Hobby|hobby]] for someone playing for fun, and a paramedic on duty is working while a bystander giving [[First aid|first aid]] is not. [[Mark Twain]]'s whitewashed-fence scene in *The Adventures of Tom Sawyer* expresses the view that the label is somewhat subjective.

Hunter-gatherers varied their effort with the seasons; agriculture brought more sustained effort, peaking at harvest. In the early modern era, Protestantism and proto-capitalism emphasized the moral advantages of hard work, and industrialization intensified demands on workers to keep pace with machines. Restrictions on working hours and the ages of workers followed. According to a 2024 study, most current U.S. employment is in occupations introduced since 1940. Economists commonly divide economies into primary (extraction), secondary (manufacturing), and tertiary (services) sectors.

Work has been tied to power, class, tradition, and rights, and dirty, dangerous, or demeaning occupations can threaten survival. Paul Lafargue, David Graeber, and Bob Black are among those who have urged reducing or abolishing it. Retirement and, more recently, experiments with universal basic income aim to end the economic necessity of lifelong work.

Global conflict (September 1, 1939–September 2, 1945) between two coalitions, the Allies and the [[Axis powers]]. Nearly all the world's countries took part, many in total war on an unprecedented scale. It was the deadliest conflict in history; estimates of deaths range from 60 million to 85 million, a majority civilians.

Causes included unresolved tensions after [[World War I]], the rise of fascism in Europe, and Japanese militarism. Most historians date the war's start to September 1, 1939, when Nazi Germany under [[Adolf Hitler]] invaded Poland and the United Kingdom and France declared war. The Soviet Union invaded Poland in mid-September, and the two states partitioned it under the [[Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact]]. France fell in June 1940. Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, opening the Eastern Front. In December 1941 Japan attacked American and British territories, including Pearl Harbor, bringing in the United States.

Japan's advance was halted at Midway in June 1942, and Axis forces were defeated in North Africa and at Stalingrad in early 1943. Germany surrendered unconditionally on May 8, 1945. On August 6 and 9 the United States dropped atomic bombs on [[Hiroshima]] and [[Nagasaki]]; Japan announced its surrender on August 15 and signed on September 2.

The war reshaped the world. The [[United Nations]] was created. The Soviet Union and the United States emerged as rival superpowers, setting the stage for the [[Cold War]], and the decline of Europe's great powers triggered decolonization in Africa and Asia.

Global conflict (July 28, 1914–November 11, 1918), also called the Great War, between the Allies (or Entente) and the [[Central Powers]]. It caused 15 to 22 million deaths, including those from war crimes and genocides, and contributed to the spread of the Spanish flu pandemic. It saw new weaponry, including machine guns, chemical weapons, and tanks.

Causes included the rise of the German Empire, which disturbed the balance of power in Europe, and imperial rivalries reflected in new alliances and an arms race. On June 28, 1914, [[Gavrilo Princip]], a Bosnian Serb, assassinated Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war on July 28, and Russia mobilized in Serbia's defense. In early August Germany declared war on Russia and France, and the United Kingdom entered after Germany invaded Belgium. The [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]] settled into fortified trenches. The Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in November.

Battles at Verdun, the Somme, and Passchendaele failed to break the stalemate. In April 1917 the United States joined the Allies after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare. The Bolsheviks seized power in the [[October Revolution]], and Soviet Russia made a separate peace in March 1918. The Allied Hundred Days Offensive, beginning in August 1918, collapsed the German front line. Facing revolution at home, Kaiser [[Wilhelm II]] abdicated on November 9, and the armistice followed on November 11.

Under the [[Treaty of Versailles]], Germany lost territory, was disarmed, and had to pay reparations. The collapse of four empires created new states including Poland, Finland, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia. The [[League of Nations]] was founded to keep peace, but its failure to manage interwar instability contributed to [[World War II]].

Act of creating a persistent, usually visual representation of language on a surface. As a structured system of communication, it is also known as written language. A set of symbols, called a script, together with the rules by which it encodes a spoken language, is a [[Writing system|writing system]]. In rare cases writing is tactile rather than visual. Its physical output, whether inscribed, mechanically transferred, or digitally represented, is called a text; construing a text is [[Reading|reading]], and the ability to read and write is [[Literacy|literacy]].

Writing systems are not languages in themselves but durable means of representing language so that it can be understood later. Language is universal across human societies, but most spoken languages are not written. Writing extends speech across space, as in correspondence, and stores it for future reading, as in libraries. It also lets people externalize their thinking in forms that are easier to reflect on, elaborate, and revise.

Writing arose independently in the ancient Near East, Egypt, China, and Mesoamerica. The earliest attested systems appeared around 3200 BC in [[Mesopotamia]] with proto-[[Cuneiform|cuneiform]], first used for accounting on clay tokens and tablets, and nearly simultaneously in Egypt with hieroglyphs. Systems later diversified into logographic, syllabic, and alphabetic forms. Writing emerged to meet the needs of societies growing in economic and social complexity: tracking produce and wealth, recording history, and administering through legal codes, census records, contracts, deeds, taxation, and treaties.

Implements have included fingers, styluses, ink brushes, pencils, and pens; surfaces have included stone and clay tablets, bamboo slips, [[Papyrus|papyrus]], wax tablets, vellum, parchment, paper, copperplate, and slate. The [[Typewriter|typewriter]] and the digital word processor let writers produce visually consistent text mechanically. Natural language generation software first produced formulaic texts such as weather forecasts and sports summaries; generative pre-trained transformers can now produce longer texts from a prompt.

Individual motivations include going beyond the limits of memory (lists, recipes, maps), spreading ideas (essays, petitions, manifestos), storytelling, maintaining social networks, business correspondence, and diaries. Digital communication such as [[Email|email]] and social media has made writing an increasingly important part of daily life. In many occupations, including law, accounting, and software design, written documentation is both the main product and the mode of work. Commerce, banking, and government rest on written documents, from contracts and tax records to national constitutions.

Conventional system for representing a particular language using a set of symbols, called a script, and the rules those symbols encode. The earliest writing systems appeared in the late 4th millennium BC. Each independently invented system emerged from proto-writing, in which a few ideographs were used in a way that could not fully encode language.

Systems are classified by how their symbols, called graphemes, relate to units of language. Phonetic systems, which include alphabets and syllabaries, use graphemes that correspond to sounds. [[Alphabet|Alphabets]] use letters that generally correspond to spoken [[Phoneme|phonemes]]: pure alphabets represent consonants and vowels, abjads generally only consonants, and abugidas consonant–vowel pairs. Syllabaries use syllabograms representing whole syllables or moras. Logographic systems use graphemes that represent units of meaning such as words or [[Morpheme|morphemes]]. Alphabets typically use fewer than 100 symbols, syllabaries and logographies hundreds or thousands.

Under most contemporary definitions, writing is a visual and tactile notation whose symbols correspond systematically to functional units of a spoken or signed language, which excludes drawings and maps. Most spoken languages have not been written, and all written languages rest on a spoken one. One language, such as Hindustani, can be written in several systems, and one system can represent several languages. [[Chinese characters]] were used to write [[Vietnamese language|Vietnamese]] from at least the 13th century until the Latin-based Vietnamese alphabet replaced them in the 20th century.

The grapheme is the basic functional unit of a writing system, comparable to the phoneme in speech; visually distinct variants of one grapheme are called allographs. [[Orthography]] is the set of rules and conventions for writing shared by a community, including spelling. English orthography, for example, uses uppercase and lowercase forms of 26 letters of the [[Latin alphabet]].

River, China; the longest in Asia and third-longest in the world. Also called the Yangzi or Chang Jiang, it rises at Jari Hill in the Tanggula Mountains of the [[Tibetan Plateau]] and flows 6,300 km (3,900 mi) generally eastward to the [[East China Sea]] near [[Shanghai]]. It is the fifth-largest river in the world by discharge volume. Its drainage basin, about 1.8 million sq km, covers one-fifth of China's land area and is home to nearly one-third of the country's population.

The river has long served for water, irrigation, transportation, industry, and war. The Yangtze Delta generates as much as 20% of China's GDP, and the basin includes cities such as [[Wuhan]] and [[Nanjing]]. The [[Three Gorges Dam]] is the largest hydroelectric power station in the world. Supporters credit it with flood control; its construction displaced over 1.3 million people and has been linked to ecological harm.

The Chinese name Cháng Jiāng means Long River. In Old Chinese the river was simply Jiang; by the [[Han dynasty]] that word meant any river, and this one was called the Great River. The English name derives from Yángzǐ Jiāng, the local name of the lower river near Yangzhou, which Europeans extended to the whole river.

The river crosses many ecosystems and shelters endemic and threatened species, including the Chinese alligator and the narrow-ridged finless porpoise. The Yangtze river dolphin (baiji) and Chinese paddlefish are extinct, and the Yangtze sturgeon is extinct in the wild. Pollution, siltation, and loss of wetlands and lakes have degraded the river, and fishing bans have been introduced to restore depleted stocks. A stretch of the upper river in western Yunnan lies within the Three Parallel Rivers of Yunnan Protected Areas, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Unit of time based on how long it takes the [[Earth]] to orbit the [[Sun]]. In scientific use, the tropical year, about 365 days, 5 hours, and 48 minutes (365.2422 mean solar days), and the sidereal year, about 20 minutes longer, are more exact. Because of the planet's [[Axial tilt|axial tilt]], a year brings the seasons; temperate regions generally recognize four, while the seasonal tropics track wet and dry seasons.

A calendar year approximates the orbital period in whole days. The [[Gregorian calendar]] uses common years of 365 days and [[Leap year|leap years]] of 366; 97 of every 400 years are leap years, giving a mean year of 365.2425 days. In the [[Julian calendar]] the mean year is 365.25 days, with a leap day added every fourth year. The Revised Julian calendar, proposed in 1923 and used in some [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Eastern Orthodox churches]], has 218 leap years every 900 years. The [[Islamic calendar]] has twelve lunar months and ignores the solar year.

The word is also applied to other periods of similar duration: the lunar year (about 354 days), the seasonal year, the fiscal year, and the academic year. It can refer to the orbital period of any astronomical object, such as the Martian year of roughly 1.88 Earth years. The unit is abbreviated y or yr; scientific literature sometimes uses the symbol a, from Latin *annus*. English *year* descends from West Saxon *ġēar* and Proto-Germanic *jǣran*.

Scientific study of animals, a primary branch of [[Biology|biology]]. It covers the structure, embryology, classification, habits, and distribution of all animals, living and extinct, and how they interact with their ecosystems. The term derives from Ancient Greek *zôion* (animal) and *lógos* (study of).

Formal zoology is usually said to originate with [[Aristotle]], who in the fourth century BC studied animals as living organisms, examined their structure and development, and divided them into those with blood, roughly the vertebrates, and those without, the invertebrates. The Roman physician [[Galen]] dissected animals to study anatomy because human dissection was prohibited; some conclusions were false, but challenging his views was considered heretical for centuries.

During the Renaissance and early modern period, renewed empiricism and the discovery of new organisms revolutionized European zoology. Andreas Vesalius and William Harvey used experiment and observation in physiology, while [[Carl Linnaeus]], Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, and Buffon began to classify the diversity of life. [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]] pioneered microscopy and revealed microorganisms, laying the groundwork for cell theory. [[Alexander von Humboldt]] studied how organisms relate to their environment, laying foundations for ecology and ethology. These strands were synthesized in [[Charles Darwin]]'s 1859 theory of evolution by natural selection.

Modern zoology addresses form and function, adaptation, relationships among groups, behavior, and ecology, and has divided into disciplines such as classification, physiology, biochemistry, and evolution. The 1953 discovery of the structure of [[DNA]] opened the field of molecular biology, leading to advances in cell biology, developmental biology, and molecular genetics.

Iranian religion centered on the [[Avesta]] and the teachings of Zarathushtra Spitama, better known by the Greek form of his name, [[Zoroaster]]. Also called Mazdayasna and Behdin, it is among the world's oldest organized faiths. Its adherents exalt [[Ahura Mazda]], an uncreated, benevolent, and all-wise deity regarded as the supreme being of the universe.

The oldest and most central part of the Avesta is the Gathas, regarded as Zoroaster's own teachings; they belong to the Yasna, the core of Zoroastrian liturgy. In the Gathas the primary dualism is ethical: a choice between Asha (truth, order) and Druj (falsehood, deceit). Spenta Mainyu, the Bountiful Spirit, is opposed by Angra Mainyu, the Destructive Spirit. A strict cosmic dualism, in which Angra Mainyu as Ahriman is a co-equal adversary of Ahura Mazda, is a later development in Middle Persian texts. Scholars disagree on whether the religion is monotheistic, polytheistic, henotheistic, or a combination. The central moral precepts are good thoughts, good words, and good deeds. Fire is held sacred as a symbol of Ahura Mazda.

The religion began in the Avestan period, possibly as early as the 2nd millennium BC, and was first recorded in the mid-6th century BC. For about a millennium it was the official religion of successive Iranian polities, from the [[Achaemenid Empire]] to the [[Sasanian Empire]]. The 7th-century [[Muslim conquest of Persia]] began its decline, and persecution prompted much of the community to migrate to the Indian subcontinent, where they became the ancestors of the [[Parsis]].

A 2012 survey estimated the worldwide population at between 111,691 and 121,962, concentrated in India, Iran, and diaspora communities.
